item.title: Agentry: Building AI Agents as React Components with JSX
item.description: Agentry is a TypeScript framework that lets you define AI agents as React components using JSX — declarative, composable, and type-safe agent orchestration.
item.content:encoded:
What Is Agentry? A Framework That Treats AI Agents as React Components

Agentry is an open-source TypeScript framework that reimagines AI agents as React components. Instead of writing imperative agent logic with chained API calls and manual state management, you define agents declaratively using JSX — the same syntax React developers use for UI components. An agent becomes a tree of <Agent>, <System>, <Tools>, and <Message> elements rendered by a custom React reconciler. Created as a Thanksgiving 2025 weekend project by Colin Dsouza, Agentry is at version 0.1.0 with 8 GitHub stars and roughly 20 monthly npm downloads. Despite its early stage, the framework introduces a genuinely novel paradigm: using React’s component model not just to render UI, but to define the agent itself.

Core Architecture — How React’s Component Model Maps to Agent Execution

At the heart of Agentry is the react-reconciler package (v0.33), the same low-level library that powers React DOM and React Native. Agentry implements a custom host config that maps React’s reconciliation cycle — mount, update, unmount — to agent lifecycle events. When you write <Agent> in JSX, the reconciler creates a host instance that manages an LLM conversation loop. When a <Tool> mounts, the reconciler registers a function call handler. When it unmounts, the tool is removed from the agent’s available tool set.

This architecture means every React concept you already know — props, state, effects, context, conditional rendering — maps directly to agent behavior. The component tree becomes the agent execution tree. State changes trigger re-renders that update the agent’s system prompt, tool list, or message history. The framework uses Zustand for internal state management and eventemitter3 for event handling during execution.

Key Features Deep Dive

Declarative Agent Definition with JSX

Agentry’s most distinctive feature is its JSX-based agent definition. Here is what a basic agent looks like:

import { Agent, System, Tools, Tool, Message } from "agentry";

function MyAgent() {
  return (
    <Agent provider="openai" model="gpt-4o">
      <System>
        You are a helpful assistant with access to tools.
      </System>
      <Tools>
        <Tool name="search" parameters={searchSchema}>
          Perform web searches
        </Tool>
        <Tool name="calculator" parameters={calcSchema}>
          Perform mathematical calculations
        </Tool>
      </Tools>
    </Agent>
  );
}

This declarative approach eliminates boilerplate. The <System> component sets the system prompt. <Tools> wraps tool definitions. Each <Tool> declares a name, Zod schema for parameters, and a description. The framework handles serialization, function calling, and response parsing automatically.

Dynamic Tools via React State

Because agents are React components, you can use useState to add or remove tools dynamically based on conversation context. This is a significant departure from static tool definitions in frameworks like LangChain or the Vercel AI SDK:

function AdaptiveAgent() {
  const [hasFileAccess, setHasFileAccess] = useState(false);

  return (
    <Agent provider="openai" model="gpt-4o">
      <System>You are a file management assistant.</System>
      <Tools>
        <Tool name="read_file" parameters={readFileSchema}>
          Read file contents
        </Tool>
        {hasFileAccess && (
          <Tool name="delete_file" parameters={deleteFileSchema}>
            Delete files from disk
          </Tool>
        )}
      </Tools>
    </Agent>
  );
}

When hasFileAccess becomes true, the delete_file tool mounts and becomes available to the LLM on the next turn. When it becomes false, the tool unmounts and the agent can no longer call it. This pattern enables fine-grained, context-aware tool access control without any imperative tool registration logic.

Subagents and Composition with AgentTool

Agentry supports hierarchical agent composition through the <AgentTool> component. You can nest agents inside other agents, with type-safe parameter passing via Zod schemas:

function ResearchAgent() {
  return (
    <Agent provider="openai" model="gpt-4o">
      <System>Coordinate research across specialists.</System>
      <Tools>
        <AgentTool
          name="web_researcher"
          agent={<WebSearchAgent />}
          parameters={z.object({ query: z.string() })}
        />
        <AgentTool
          name="data_analyst"
          agent={<DataAnalysisAgent />}
          parameters={z.object({ dataset: z.string() })}
        />
      </Tools>
    </Agent>
  );
}

The parent agent calls subagents as tools. Each subagent runs its own conversation loop with its own system prompt, tools, and model configuration. The parent receives the subagent’s final output as the tool result. This mirrors the manager-employee pattern common in production agent deployments.

Conditional Rendering with Condition

Agentry includes a <Condition> component that evaluates natural language conditions against conversation history to change agent behavior:

function CustomerSupportAgent() {
  return (
    <Agent provider="openai" model="gpt-4o">
      <System>You are a customer support agent.</System>
      <Condition when="the user is frustrated or angry">
        <System>Escalate to a human supervisor and apologize.</System>
        <Tool name="escalate" parameters={escalateSchema}>
          Escalate to human support
        </Tool>
      </Condition>
      <Condition when="the user asks about pricing">
        <System>Provide pricing information from our current plans.</System>
        <Tool name="lookup_pricing" parameters={pricingSchema}>
          Look up current pricing
        </Tool>
      </Condition>
    </Agent>
  );
}

The <Condition when="natural language description"> component evaluates the condition against the conversation history using an LLM call. When the condition is met, the children mount and become active. When it is not, they unmount. This enables natural language routing — a more flexible alternative to rigid if/else logic in agent code.

Programmatic Agent Spawning

Beyond declarative composition, Agentry provides context.runAgent() for programmatic agent spawning from within tool handlers. This enables parallel execution patterns:

async function researchTask({ queries }, context) {
  const results = await Promise.all(
    queries.map((q) =>
      context.runAgent(
        <WebSearchAgent query={q} />,
        { provider: "openai", model: "gpt-4o-mini" }
      )
    )
  );
  return synthesize(results);
}

This pattern is powerful for parallelizable workloads — analyzing multiple documents, searching across sources, or running independent validation checks simultaneously. Each spawned agent runs in its own execution context with its own conversation state.

Cross-Provider Subagents

Agentry supports mixing different LLM providers in the same agent tree. An OpenAI parent agent can spawn Anthropic subagents and vice versa:

function HybridAgent() {
  return (
    <Agent provider="openai" model="gpt-4o">
      <System>Coordinate research across providers.</System>
      <Tools>
        <AgentTool
          name="claude_analyst"
          agent={
            <Agent provider="anthropic" model="claude-sonnet-4">
              <System>Analyze data with deep reasoning.</System>
            </Agent>
          }
          parameters={z.object({ data: z.string() })}
        />
      </Tools>
    </Agent>
  );
}

This cross-provider capability is rare among agent frameworks. Most frameworks lock you into a single provider. Agentry’s provider-agnostic reconciler means each subagent can use the model best suited to its task — GPT-4o for tool use, Claude for reasoning, a smaller model for classification — all within a single declarative tree.

Streaming and WebSocket Mode

Agentry supports both batch mode (run to completion and return the final result) and interactive mode (streaming responses with an ongoing conversation handle). For OpenAI, it offers WebSocket mode that reduces latency in multi-tool loops by maintaining a persistent connection. The framework also includes compaction controls for long conversations — you can configure when and how aggressively to summarize older messages to stay within context limits. Anthropic’s prompt caching is supported out of the box.

Comparison with Alternatives

Feature Agentry Tambo Vercel AI SDK
Approach Agents as React components Agents render React components Generative UI + agent tools
Stars 8 11,157 25,910
npm downloads/month ~20 Thousands Millions
Release v0.1.0 (Dec 2025) v1.0 (Feb 2026) v4.x (stable)
JSX agent definition Yes — core paradigm No No
Dynamic tools via state Yes — React useState No Limited
Subagents Yes — AgentTool + runAgent Yes Via AI SDK
Cross-provider Yes — mix OpenAI/Anthropic No Yes
Conditional routing Yes — Condition component No No
Streaming Yes — batch + interactive Yes Yes
WebSocket mode Yes (OpenAI) No Yes
Prompt caching Yes (Anthropic) Yes Yes
Maturity Experimental Production-ready Production-ready

Tambo — Agents That Render React Components

Tambo (11,157 stars) takes the opposite approach from Agentry. Instead of agents being React components, Tambo gives agents the ability to render React components. An agent decides which UI component to show based on conversation context, and Tambo handles the state management between the user, the agent, and the rendered component. Tambo has processed over half a million messages on its hosted service and reached v1.0 in February 2026. It is significantly more mature than Agentry and has an active community.

Vercel AI SDK — The Industry Standard

The Vercel AI SDK (25,910 stars) is the dominant toolkit for building AI-powered applications in the TypeScript ecosystem. Created by the team behind Next.js, it supports generative UI — agents that dynamically render React components — alongside streaming, tool calling, and multi-model support. It is framework-agnostic (React, Svelte, Vue, Next.js) and production-tested at scale. For most teams, the Vercel AI SDK is the safe, proven choice.

Agent Prism and Gaia UI — Visualization and UI Libraries

Agent Prism (376 stars) by Evil Martians focuses on observability — visualizing AI agent traces using OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing of LLM calls. Gaia UI (212 stars) provides beautifully designed React components for building agent interfaces. Neither competes directly with Agentry; they solve different problems in the agent development stack.

Practical Evaluation — Installation, Setup, and First Impressions

Agentry requires React 19 and Zod 4 as peer dependencies, plus either the Anthropic or OpenAI SDK depending on your provider. Installation is straightforward:

npm install agentry

The framework ships as a single small package with minimal dependencies: react-reconciler, zustand, eventemitter3, and scheduler. The API surface is compact — you can learn the core concepts in under 30 minutes if you already know React and TypeScript.

However, documentation is sparse. The README on GitHub provides examples but no API reference, no migration guide, and no troubleshooting section. There are no tests visible in the repository, no CI/CD pipeline, and no contribution guidelines. For a framework at v0.1.0, this is expected but worth noting.

Use Cases and When to Use Agentry

Agentry’s declarative, component-based approach shines in specific scenarios:

  • Complex agent hierarchies — When you need manager agents that delegate to specialist subagents with different models and tools
  • Dynamic tool access control — When tool availability depends on context, authentication state, or user role
  • Multi-provider agent systems — When different subtasks benefit from different LLM providers
  • Experimental and research projects — When you want to explore novel agent composition patterns
  • React-centric teams — When your team already thinks in components and wants to apply that mental model to agents

For production applications serving real users, Tambo or the Vercel AI SDK are safer choices today. Agentry is best suited for exploration, prototyping, and understanding what declarative agent composition looks like in practice.

Limitations and Maturity Concerns

Agentry’s biggest limitation is its maturity. With 8 GitHub stars, 20 monthly npm downloads, and no visible test suite, the framework is effectively an experimental prototype. Key concerns include:

  • No production deployments — No evidence of the framework running in production
  • Single maintainer — Colin Dsouza is the sole contributor; bus factor of 1
  • No test coverage — No tests visible in the repository
  • No documentation beyond README — No API docs, no examples directory, no guides
  • React 19 requirement — Teams on React 18 cannot adopt Agentry without upgrading
  • Zod 4 requirement — Zod 4 is still in early adoption; many projects use Zod 3
  • No error handling guidance — How does the framework handle provider failures, rate limits, or malformed tool calls?
  • No streaming reliability guarantees — WebSocket reconnection, backpressure, and error recovery are undocumented

Verdict — Is Agentry Worth Adopting?

Agentry is one of the most interesting experimental agent frameworks in the TypeScript ecosystem. Its core insight — that React’s component model maps naturally to agent composition — is genuinely novel and could influence how future agent frameworks are designed. The ability to define agents with JSX, manage tools with useState, compose subagents declaratively, and mix providers in a single tree is powerful.

However, Agentry is not production-ready. At v0.1.0 with 8 stars and no test coverage, it is a proof of concept — a glimpse of what declarative agent composition could look like, not a tool for building production systems. For teams building agent-powered applications today, the Vercel AI SDK or Tambo are the right choices. For teams curious about where agent frameworks are heading, Agentry is worth watching — and perhaps contributing to.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Agentry and how does it work?

Agentry is a TypeScript framework that lets you define AI agents as React components using JSX syntax. It uses React’s reconciler to render agent execution trees, mapping React’s component lifecycle to agent lifecycle events. Agents are composed declaratively with components like <Agent>, <System>, <Tools>, and <Message>.

How is Agentry different from the Vercel AI SDK?

The Vercel AI SDK provides tools for building AI-powered applications with generative UI — agents that can render React components. Agentry takes the opposite approach: the agent itself is a React component. Agentry also supports JSX-based agent definitions, dynamic tool mounting via React state, and cross-provider subagents as first-class features.

Does Agentry support multiple LLM providers?

Yes. Agentry supports both OpenAI and Anthropic providers through a single declarative API. It also supports cross-provider subagents — an OpenAI parent agent can spawn Anthropic subagents and vice versa. Each subagent in the tree can use a different provider and model.

Is Agentry ready for production use?

No. Agentry is at version 0.1.0 with 8 GitHub stars, approximately 20 monthly npm downloads, no visible test suite, and a single maintainer. It is best suited for experimentation, prototyping, and research. For production applications, consider the Vercel AI SDK or Tambo.

What are the prerequisites for using Agentry?

Agentry requires React 19 and Zod 4 as peer dependencies, plus either the Anthropic SDK or OpenAI SDK depending on your chosen provider. The framework itself has minimal dependencies: react-reconciler, zustand, eventemitter3, and scheduler.

item.title: AI Agent Framework Comparison 2026: Mastra vs Agno vs LangGraph vs CrewAI
item.description: Compare the top 4 AI agent frameworks of 2026 — Mastra, Agno, LangGraph, and CrewAI — across language support, orchestration, production readiness, and community size.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction — The AI Agent Framework Landscape in 2026

The AI agent framework landscape in 2026 has matured dramatically from the experimental AutoGPT era of 2023. Four frameworks now dominate the conversation: Mastra (26.4k GitHub stars), Agno (41.3k stars), LangGraph (37.7k stars), and CrewAI (55.9k stars). Each takes a fundamentally different approach to building, orchestrating, and deploying AI agents. This AI agent framework comparison 2026 guide breaks down their architectures, strengths, weaknesses, and ideal use cases so you can choose the right tool for your next project.

Why Agent Frameworks Matter — From AutoGPT to Production-Grade Systems

The shift from experimental single-agent prototypes to production-grade multi-agent systems has been the defining trend of 2024–2026. Early frameworks like AutoGPT proved that LLM-driven agents could autonomously pursue goals, but they lacked the reliability, state management, and observability that enterprises demand.

Today’s agent frameworks solve four critical problems:

  1. Orchestration — Coordinating multiple agents that communicate, delegate, and hand off tasks
  2. State management — Persisting conversation history, tool outputs, and agent memory across sessions
  3. Tool integration — Connecting agents to APIs, databases, and external services with reliable function calling
  4. Observability — Tracing agent decisions, LLM calls, and tool executions for debugging and compliance

According to the CrewAI 2026 State of Agentic AI Survey, 65% of enterprises already use AI agents, and 81% are scaling them across teams. The question is no longer whether to adopt agent frameworks — it’s which one to standardize on.

Framework Deep Dives

Mastra — The TypeScript-Native Contender (26.4k ★)

Mastra launched in August 2024 and has rapidly grown to 26.4k GitHub stars with 2.5k forks. It is the only major framework built from the ground up for TypeScript, making it the default choice for JavaScript/TypeScript development teams.

Key features:

  • Native TypeScript support with full type safety across agent definitions, tools, and workflows
  • Built-in observability via Mastra Studio — a visual debugger for agent traces and LLM calls
  • Workflow engine supporting sequential, parallel, and conditional execution paths
  • Memory management with support for working memory, long-term storage, and semantic recall
  • First-class deployment integrations with Vercel, Cloudflare Workers, and Node.js servers

Mastra’s strength is its developer experience for TypeScript teams. If your stack is built on Next.js, Node.js, or any JS/TS ecosystem, Mastra integrates without introducing a new language. Its built-in observability tooling means you don’t need to bolt on a separate monitoring solution.

Best for: TypeScript/JavaScript teams, full-stack developers, projects that need built-in observability from day one.

Limitations: Smaller community than CrewAI or LangGraph; Python teams will need to maintain a separate stack; fewer production case studies compared to more mature frameworks.

Agno — SDK + Runtime Separation (41.3k ★)

Agno (formerly Phidata) has taken a unique architectural stance: it separates the agent framework (Agno SDK) from the agent runtime (AgentOS). This decoupling is the most forward-looking design in the current landscape.

Key features:

  • Agno SDK — A Python framework for defining agents, tools, workflows, and knowledge bases
  • AgentOS — A framework-agnostic runtime/control plane for deploying, monitoring, and managing agents in production
  • Multi-agent orchestration with role-based delegation and parallel execution
  • Built-in knowledge base integration with vector databases (Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate)
  • Tool-calling reliability improvements over raw LLM function calling

Agno’s core insight, articulated in their blog post “The Framework Wars Are Over (And Nobody Won),” is that switching costs are high because most frameworks bundle orchestration code with deployment infrastructure. By decoupling the two, Agno lets teams switch orchestration patterns — or even frameworks — without re-platforming their production infrastructure.

Best for: Teams that value architectural flexibility, Python-heavy organizations, projects that need framework-agnostic production infrastructure.

Limitations: AgentOS is newer and has fewer battle-tested deployments; the two-component architecture adds conceptual overhead; smaller ecosystem of community-built tools compared to LangGraph or CrewAI.

LangGraph — Low-Level Orchestration Powerhouse (37.7k ★)

LangGraph, built by the LangChain team, is the most powerful and flexible agent orchestration framework available. With 37.7k GitHub stars and 6.3k forks, it has the deepest integration with the LangChain ecosystem.

Key features:

  • Graph-based state machine architecture — agents are nodes, transitions are edges
  • Full control over agent state, routing, and execution flow
  • Built-in persistence with checkpointing, thread-level state, and human-in-the-loop support
  • LangSmith integration for production-grade observability and tracing
  • Used in production by Klarna, Uber, and J.P. Morgan

LangGraph’s graph-based approach gives developers complete control over agent behavior. You define nodes (agent actions, tool calls, decision points) and edges (transitions between nodes), creating a directed graph that the runtime executes. This makes it ideal for complex workflows where agents must follow strict business logic, maintain state across multiple turns, or support human approval gates.

Best for: Complex multi-agent orchestration, production systems requiring fine-grained control, teams already invested in the LangChain ecosystem.

Limitations: Steepest learning curve of all four frameworks; graph-based programming model is unfamiliar to many developers; heavier boilerplate for simple use cases; LangChain dependency chain can be complex to manage.

CrewAI — The Community Favorite for Multi-Agent (55.9k ★)

CrewAI is the most popular AI agent framework by GitHub stars (55.9k) and forks (7.9k). Its role-based abstraction — where you define agents with roles, goals, and backstories — makes multi-agent systems intuitive and accessible.

Key features:

  • Role-based agent design — define agents as “researcher,” “writer,” “critic” with specific goals
  • Built-in task delegation and hierarchical process management
  • Sequential and hierarchical workflow patterns
  • Integration with over 1,000+ tools via the CrewAI tool ecosystem
  • YAML-based configuration for agent and task definitions

CrewAI’s strength is its simplicity. A developer can define a multi-agent research team in under 50 lines of code. The role-playing abstraction maps naturally to business workflows — a marketing team with a strategist, copywriter, and editor translates directly into CrewAI agents.

Best for: Rapid prototyping, role-based multi-agent scenarios, teams new to agent development, projects that need to ship quickly.

Limitations: Opinionated architecture limits customization for complex workflows; less suitable for production systems requiring fine-grained state control; performance overhead from the abstraction layer; fewer built-in observability features compared to Mastra or LangGraph.

Head-to-Head Comparison Matrix

Feature Mastra Agno LangGraph CrewAI
Language TypeScript Python Python Python
GitHub Stars 26.4k 41.3k 37.7k 55.9k
Forks 2.5k 5.7k 6.3k 7.9k
Release Year 2024 2023 (rebranded 2025) 2024 2023
Orchestration Model Workflow engine SDK + Runtime Graph-based state machine Role-based agents
Built-in Observability Yes (Mastra Studio) Yes (AgentOS) Yes (LangSmith) Limited (third-party)
Memory/State Working + long-term Knowledge base + memory Checkpointing + threads Task-based context
Production Deployments Growing Early Klarna, Uber, J.P. Morgan Many startups
Learning Curve Low-Medium Medium High Low
Best For TypeScript teams Flexible architecture Complex orchestration Rapid prototyping

Language Support (TypeScript vs Python)

The language divide is the single most important decision factor. Mastra is the only TypeScript-native framework, while Agno, LangGraph, and CrewAI are all Python-first.

For TypeScript/JavaScript teams, Mastra eliminates the need to maintain a separate Python codebase for agent development. It integrates naturally with Next.js, Node.js, Vercel, and Cloudflare Workers — the modern full-stack JavaScript stack.

Python teams have three strong options. Agno offers the most architectural flexibility with its SDK + runtime separation. LangGraph provides the deepest control for complex workflows. CrewAI delivers the fastest path from idea to working prototype.

The choice often comes down to your team’s existing expertise. A Node.js backend team will find Mastra’s TypeScript-native approach dramatically more productive than learning Python and the LangChain ecosystem.

Learning Curve & Developer Experience

CrewAI wins on ease of use. Its role-based abstraction is intuitive — anyone who has worked in a team can understand “researcher agent,” “writer agent,” “critic agent.” The YAML configuration format makes agent definitions readable and maintainable.

Mastra offers a close second, especially for TypeScript developers. Type safety catches errors at compile time, and the built-in Studio provides visual debugging that reduces iteration time.

Agno sits in the middle. The SDK is straightforward, but the two-component architecture (SDK + AgentOS) requires understanding a broader mental model.

LangGraph has the steepest learning curve. The graph-based state machine model is powerful but requires a paradigm shift for most developers. You’re not writing linear code — you’re defining nodes, edges, routing functions, and state schemas. The payoff is complete control, but the upfront investment is significant.

Production Readiness & Deployment

LangGraph leads in production readiness, with documented deployments at Klarna, Uber, and J.P. Morgan. Its checkpointing, human-in-the-loop support, and LangSmith observability make it suitable for regulated industries.

Mastra’s built-in deployment integrations with Vercel and Cloudflare Workers make it the easiest to deploy for web applications. The Mastra Studio provides production-grade observability without additional infrastructure.

Agno’s AgentOS is designed specifically for production deployment, with a control plane for monitoring, scaling, and managing agents. However, it’s newer and has fewer documented large-scale deployments.

CrewAI is widely used in production by startups and mid-market companies, but its opinionated architecture can be a limitation for complex enterprise requirements. The lack of built-in observability means teams need to add their own monitoring.

Multi-Agent Orchestration Patterns

The four frameworks take fundamentally different approaches to multi-agent orchestration:

  • LangGraph uses a graph-based state machine where agents are nodes and transitions are edges. This gives maximum control but requires explicit definition of every state and transition.

  • CrewAI uses role-based hierarchical orchestration. Agents have roles, goals, and backstories, and tasks are assigned through sequential or hierarchical processes.

  • Agno supports role-based delegation with parallel execution, plus the ability to switch orchestration patterns through its decoupled architecture.

  • Mastra uses a workflow engine with sequential, parallel, and conditional execution paths, all defined in TypeScript with full type safety.

For simple sequential workflows, all four frameworks work well. For complex branching logic with conditional routing, LangGraph’s graph model excels. For rapid multi-agent prototyping, CrewAI’s role-based approach is unmatched.

Memory, State & Persistence

Memory management is a critical differentiator for production agent systems:

  • LangGraph offers the most sophisticated state management with checkpointing, thread-level persistence, and the ability to pause/resume agent execution. This is essential for long-running agent workflows.

  • Agno provides knowledge base integration with vector databases and built-in memory management, making it strong for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) use cases.

  • Mastra supports working memory (short-term context) and long-term storage with semantic recall, suitable for most conversational agent use cases.

  • CrewAI uses task-based context passing — agents share information through task outputs. This works well for sequential workflows but is less suitable for agents that need persistent memory across sessions.

Observability & Monitoring

Observability is where the frameworks diverge most:

  • Mastra Studio provides visual debugging of agent traces, LLM calls, and tool executions out of the box. No additional setup required.

  • LangGraph integrates with LangSmith for comprehensive tracing, monitoring, and evaluation. LangSmith is a separate product but deeply integrated.

  • Agno includes observability through AgentOS, with monitoring dashboards and execution traces.

  • CrewAI has limited built-in observability. Teams typically add Langfuse, LangSmith, or custom logging.

For teams that prioritize debugging and monitoring, Mastra’s built-in Studio and LangGraph’s LangSmith integration provide the most polished experiences.

Community & Ecosystem Size

CrewAI leads with 55.9k GitHub stars and the largest community. This translates to more tutorials, community-built tools, and faster answers to questions.

LangGraph benefits from the broader LangChain ecosystem, which includes LangSmith, LangServe, and extensive documentation. The LangChain community is one of the largest in the AI development space.

Agno (41.3k stars) has a growing community, particularly among developers interested in the decoupled architecture approach.

Mastra (26.4k stars) has the smallest community but is growing rapidly. Its TypeScript focus means it attracts a different developer demographic than the Python-dominated alternatives.

The Framework Wars Are Over — Orchestration vs. Runtime Decoupling

Agno’s provocative thesis — that the framework wars are over and nobody won — captures a crucial insight. The real architectural distinction isn’t between frameworks but between orchestration and runtime.

Most frameworks bundle both layers together. When you build with CrewAI, you’re locked into CrewAI’s deployment model. When you build with LangGraph, you’re locked into the LangChain ecosystem. This bundling creates high switching costs — migrating from one framework to another means rewriting both your agent logic and your deployment infrastructure.

Agno’s AgentOS is the first serious attempt to decouple these layers. AgentOS provides a framework-agnostic runtime that can execute agents built with any orchestration framework. If you build your agent logic with Agno SDK but deploy on AgentOS, you can theoretically switch to a different orchestration pattern without touching your production infrastructure.

This decoupling pattern mirrors the evolution of web development, where frameworks (React, Vue, Angular) are separate from deployment platforms (Vercel, Netlify, AWS). The same separation is now emerging in the agent framework space.

Enterprise Adoption Trends — What the 2026 Data Says

The CrewAI 2026 State of Agentic AI Survey, conducted among 500 senior enterprise executives, reveals a market at an inflection point:

  • 100% of surveyed enterprises plan to expand agentic AI adoption in 2026
  • 65% are already using AI agents in production
  • 81% are scaling agent deployments across multiple teams
  • 75% report high or very high impact on time savings
  • 69% cite significant operational cost reductions
  • 34% rank security and governance as the top evaluation factor for agentic platforms
  • 57% prefer building on existing open-source tools rather than building from scratch

The security and governance finding is particularly significant. In 2024 and 2025, the primary evaluation criteria were raw capability and ease of use. In 2026, enterprises are prioritizing security, compliance, and governance — a sign that agentic AI has moved from experimental to mission-critical.

How to Choose the Right Framework for Your Use Case

Choose Mastra if: Your team is TypeScript/JavaScript-native, you want built-in observability without additional tooling, or you’re deploying on Vercel/Cloudflare Workers.

Choose Agno if: You value architectural flexibility, want to decouple orchestration from runtime, or need strong knowledge base/RAG integration.

Choose LangGraph if: You’re building complex multi-agent systems with strict state management requirements, need human-in-the-loop workflows, or are already invested in the LangChain ecosystem.

Choose CrewAI if: You need to prototype and ship multi-agent systems quickly, your use case maps naturally to role-based agents, or you want the largest community and ecosystem.

For most teams, the decision comes down to language preference (TypeScript vs. Python) and complexity requirements. Simple to moderately complex agent systems can be built with any framework. For production systems with complex state management, LangGraph or Mastra are the strongest choices. For rapid experimentation and prototyping, CrewAI is unmatched.

Conclusion — The Future of AI Agent Frameworks

The AI agent framework landscape in 2026 is defined by four strong contenders, each with a distinct architectural philosophy. Mastra brings TypeScript-native development with built-in observability. Agno pioneers the orchestration-runtime decoupling. LangGraph offers unmatched control for complex production systems. CrewAI makes multi-agent development accessible to everyone.

The most important trend is the maturation of the ecosystem. Enterprise adoption has reached a tipping point — 100% of enterprises plan to expand agentic AI in 2026. Security and governance have overtaken raw capability as the primary evaluation criteria. And the architectural debate is shifting from “which framework” to “how to decouple orchestration from runtime.”

As the market matures, expect to see more convergence on the decoupled architecture that Agno is pioneering, with frameworks specializing in orchestration while runtimes specialize in production deployment. The framework wars may indeed be over — but the real battle for production-grade agent infrastructure is just beginning.

FAQ

Q1: What is the best AI agent framework in 2026? A: There is no single “best” framework — the right choice depends on your team’s language preference, complexity requirements, and deployment needs. Mastra is best for TypeScript teams, LangGraph for complex orchestration, CrewAI for rapid prototyping, and Agno for architectural flexibility.

Q2: Is CrewAI better than LangGraph? A: CrewAI is better for rapid prototyping and role-based multi-agent scenarios, while LangGraph is better for complex production systems requiring fine-grained state control. CrewAI has more GitHub stars (55.9k vs 37.7k), but LangGraph has more production deployments at enterprise scale.

Q3: Can I use Mastra with Python? A: No — Mastra is TypeScript-native and does not support Python. If your team uses Python, consider Agno, LangGraph, or CrewAI instead.

Q4: What is the difference between agent orchestration and agent runtime? A: Orchestration refers to how agents are defined, coordinated, and how they communicate. Runtime refers to the production infrastructure for deploying, monitoring, and scaling agents. Most frameworks bundle both, but Agno’s AgentOS decouples them, allowing teams to switch orchestration patterns without changing deployment infrastructure.

Q5: How do I choose between Agno and CrewAI? A: Choose Agno if you value architectural flexibility, want to decouple orchestration from runtime, or need strong knowledge base integration. Choose CrewAI if you need to prototype quickly, prefer role-based agent abstractions, or want the largest community and ecosystem.

item.title: Your Agents Should Be Multiplayer: Collaborative AI Workflows (2026)
item.description: Single-agent AI is hitting a wall. Here's why the next frontier is agent teams — and the protocols, tools, and patterns that make multiplayer AI workflows work in production.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve been running production AI agent systems for over a year now, and the single biggest shift I’ve seen in 2026 is this: the best agents don’t work alone. The teams getting real leverage out of AI aren’t the ones with one super-agent — they’re the ones running five, ten, or twenty specialized agents that talk to each other.

This isn’t a prediction. It’s already happening. Meta’s HyperAgents paper (arXiv:2603.19461) proved that multi-agent systems can solve problems no single agent can touch. A production field study from Calx showed six agents building 82,000 lines of code in 20 days for $250. And the infrastructure to make this work — protocols, SDKs, open-source orchestrators — is already here, just not widely adopted yet.

Let me walk through what “multiplayer AI” actually means in practice, the stack that makes it work, and the hard lessons I’ve learned about where it breaks.

The Multiplayer Paradigm Shift

Think about how you actually build software. You don’t have one developer do everything. You have a frontend person, a backend person, someone on DevOps, a reviewer. They talk in Slack, leave PR comments, sync on architecture decisions. The whole is smarter than any individual.

AI agents work the same way — or at least, they should. A single agent has a context window, a tool set, and a personality (its system prompt). Ask it to do everything and you get a jack-of-all-trades that’s mediocre at each task. Specialize your agents — one for research, one for code generation, one for review, one for deployment — and suddenly each one can be excellent at its job.

The gaming analogy is apt. We went from single-player (one agent, one session) to local multiplayer (multiple agents on the same machine) to online multiplayer (agents across machines, communicating over protocols). Most teams are still in the single-player era. The ones who’ve moved to multiplayer are seeing 3-4x throughput improvements.

The Emerging Protocol Stack: MCP + A2A

The biggest question when I started building multi-agent systems was: how do they talk to each other? The answer in 2026 is a two-protocol stack that’s rapidly becoming standard.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) — Anthropic’s protocol for agents to access tools. Your agent talks to a database, a file system, an API. MCP is the “how do I interact with the world” layer.

A2A (Agent-to-Agent Protocol) — Google’s protocol, donated to the Linux Foundation in June 2025, for agents to talk to other agents. A2A is the “how do I coordinate with my peers” layer.

I’ve written a detailed comparison of MCP vs A2A if you want the full technical breakdown, but the short version is: you need both. MCP without A2A means your agent can use tools but can’t delegate work. A2A without MCP means your agents can talk but can’t do anything useful.

In production, I run agents that expose both interfaces. A research agent exposes an A2A endpoint that other agents call with “research this topic and return a brief.” Internally, that agent uses MCP to query web search, read documentation, and write files. The calling agent never needs to know about those tools — it just sends an A2A message and gets a result back.

What HyperAgents and the Calx Study Actually Tell Us

Meta’s HyperAgents paper dropped in March 2026 and it’s one of those papers that changes how you think about agent architecture. The headline finding: on math transfer tasks, HyperAgents achieved imp@50 = 0.630 where traditional transfer methods scored 0.0. That’s not an incremental improvement — it’s a phase change.

The key insight is that documentation is not behavior. You can write the most detailed system prompt in the world, but an agent won’t actually follow it the way you expect. Meta found that executable mechanisms — actual code, rules enforced at runtime, behavioral guardrails — transfer agent improvement across domains. Written rules don’t.

The Calx field study drives this home with real numbers. A team ran six AI agents that built 82,000 lines of code in 20 days for $250. Impressive, right? But when they transferred 237 correction rules to a new agent, it still made 44 new mistakes — 13 of which were in categories the rules explicitly covered. The rules were documented. The agent just didn’t follow them.

This is the single most important lesson for multi-agent systems: don’t trust prompts to enforce behavior. If you want an agent to follow a rule, make it executable. Use runtime validation, output guards, and tool-level constraints. A prompt is a suggestion. A code check is a guarantee.

Claude Code’s Hidden Multi-Agent Infrastructure

Here’s something that surprised me: Claude Code’s agent SDK already ships with full multi-agent coordination built in. I’m talking about in-process agent runners, mailbox messaging between agents, team-based architecture with team leads, and shutdown coordination. It’s all there in @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk.

Most people use Claude Code as a single-agent REPL. You type a prompt, it does a thing. But the SDK supports spawning child agents, routing messages between them, and coordinating work across a team of agents. The infrastructure for multiplayer agents is already in your node_modules — most people just haven’t wired it up.

I’ve been running a setup where a “team lead” agent receives a task, breaks it into subtasks, and dispatches each one to a specialized child agent. The research agent gathers context, the coding agent writes code, the review agent checks for issues, and the documentation agent writes the docs. They communicate through the SDK’s mailbox system. The team lead handles conflicts and merges results.

If you’re already using Claude Code, you’re one config file away from a multi-agent setup. The SDK documentation covers the AgentTeam, AgentRunner, and Mailbox classes. Start there.

The Open-Source Ecosystem

The protocol stack and commercial SDKs are one path. But the open-source ecosystem is where the real experimentation is happening, and it’s moving fast.

OpenSwarm is an open-source multi-agent Claude CLI orchestrator that coordinates multiple Claude Code agents as a team with task distribution. It hit 34 points on Hacker News — strong community interest in this space. It’s designed for Linear/GitHub workflows, which makes sense: those are the most common multi-agent use cases right now.

Egregore tackles the isolation problem head-on. Every Claude Code session starts from scratch — no memory of what happened before. Egregore provides shared memory and coordination for multiplayer Claude Code sessions. If you’ve ever had an agent redo work because it didn’t remember what another agent already did, you know exactly why this matters.

Muster takes a different approach entirely. It’s a multi-agent product team built on markdown files. The coordination layer is literally .md files — agents write plans, specs, and status updates to markdown, and other agents read them. It’s lightweight, zero-infrastructure, and surprisingly effective. I’ve used this pattern myself for quick experiments before investing in a full protocol stack.

I covered the major frameworks in my multi-agent framework comparison, but the open-source tools above are worth watching because they’re solving real pain points that the big frameworks don’t address.

Real-World Use Cases

Let me give you three patterns I’ve seen work in production.

Code review pipelines. One agent writes code, another reviews it. The reviewer agent has a different system prompt, different tools (security scanner, linter, style checker), and a different temperature setting. It catches things the writer agent misses because it’s looking at the code from a different angle. I’ve seen this catch subtle race conditions and security issues that a single agent would have missed.

Document collaboration. Platforms like odocs are pioneering multiplayer doc editing where humans and AI agents edit together in real-time. Partial document updates preserve version history without full rewrites — a critical feature when you have multiple agents touching the same document. Agents can share context directly to other agents through the platform, which solves the “I need to know what agent B already figured out” problem.

Research-to-code pipelines. A research agent gathers context, a planning agent creates a spec, a coding agent implements it, and a testing agent validates it. Each agent passes artifacts to the next through A2A messages or shared files. I run this exact pipeline for my blog’s content production — a strategist agent identifies topics, a researcher gathers data, a writer drafts the post, and a publisher deploys it. Each agent is specialized and excellent at its one job.

The Trust Layer Problem

Here’s the hard truth: multi-agent systems introduce trust problems that single-agent systems don’t have.

When you have one agent, you review its output. When you have ten agents, you can’t review everything. You need automated trust mechanisms.

The Calx approach — tracking corrections and compiling them into enforced rules — is one solution. Every time a human corrects an agent’s output, that correction becomes a rule that all agents in the system must follow. It’s executable, not documented. It’s enforced at the tool level, not the prompt level.

Another approach is the behavioral guardrail pattern. Each agent has a “guard” that validates its output before passing it to the next agent. The guard checks for policy violations, security issues, and format compliance. If the output fails, the agent retries with the guard’s feedback. This is the pattern I use in production, and it catches about 95% of issues before they propagate.

The remaining 5% require human review. The trick is knowing which 5% — and that’s where correction tracking becomes essential. Log every agent output, every human correction, and use that data to improve your guards.

The Road Ahead

Looking at 2027, I see three trends that will define multiplayer AI workflows.

First, protocol consolidation. MCP and A2A are winning, but there’s still fragmentation in how agents discover each other, authenticate, and negotiate capabilities. Expect a registry layer — something like a DNS for agents — to emerge.

Second, behavioral guardrails become standard. The HyperAgents insight — documentation is not behavior — will drive a new category of tools that enforce agent behavior at runtime. Every production multi-agent system will have a guard layer.

Third, the cost curve flips. Right now, running multiple agents costs more than running one. But as models get cheaper and specialized small models outperform general large models on specific tasks, running a team of specialized agents will be cheaper than one generalist agent. The Calx study already hints at this: $250 for 82,000 lines of code across six agents. That math gets better every quarter.

If you’re still running single-agent workflows, start experimenting with multiplayer patterns today. Wire up two agents that talk to each other. Add a reviewer agent to your code generation pipeline. Try the Claude Code SDK’s team features. The infrastructure is ready. The protocols are stable. The only thing missing is your architecture.

For more context on how to set up parallel agent workflows, check out my multi-agent coding workflow guide — it covers the practical setup patterns I use daily.
